summary: Chinese has two everyday negators, placed directly before the verb (or before 在 + place). 不 bù negates will, habits, likes, the present and the future, adjectives and 是: 我不吃肉 ‘I don’t eat meat’. 没 méi (often 没有) negates 有 and says that something did not happen or has not happened yet: 我没吃早饭 ‘I didn’t have breakfast’, 我没有咖啡 ‘I have no coffee’. There is no ‘do’, the verb does not change, and there is no word ‘no’ before a noun (German kein): 没有 + noun does it. ‘Nothing’, ‘nobody’ and ‘never’ are built with the same two negators — 什么都不 / 什么都没, 没有人, 从来不 / 从来没 — and ‘neither … nor’ is 不 …，也不 ….

head: Meaning
Negator
Example
rows: 我不喝咖啡。 I don’t drink coffee.
这不是糖。 This isn’t sugar.
他不在家。 He isn’t at home.
我没有牛奶。 I have no milk.
他没吃早饭。 He didn’t have breakfast.

items.title: 不 — will, habit, state
points: 他不吃鱼。 He doesn’t eat fish (never does / won’t).
Also with 是, 在 and adjectives.

items.title: 没 — fact, event
points: 他没吃鱼。 He didn’t eat the fish (it didn’t happen).

head: English
Chinese
Example
rows: 我没有面包。 I have no bread.
什么都不 / 什么都没
他什么都不吃。 He eats nothing. — 她什么都没买。 She bought nothing.
没有人在家。 Nobody is at home.
从来不 / 从来没 … 过 (S14)
我从来不喝咖啡。 I never drink coffee.
我不喝茶，也不喝咖啡。 I drink neither tea nor coffee.
blocks.caption: Nothing, nobody, never, neither … nor

blocks.title: The verb is always negated
blocks.text: Like Greek δεν … τίποτα and Russian ничего не …, Chinese negates the verb: 什么都 alone means ‘everything’, 什么都 + 不 + verb ‘nothing’. German nichts or niemand need no nicht — Chinese always needs 不 or 没.

blocks.title: Where the negation goes
blocks.text: Right before the verb, after 都, 也, 从来 and 什么都: 我们都不喝, 他从来不吃肉, 她什么都没买. Note 都不 ‘none (of us)’ vs 不都 ‘not all (of us)’.

blocks.title: bù or bú?
blocks.text: 不 is said bú before a 4th tone: 不是 bú shì, 不要 bú yào, 不在 bú zài; bù elsewhere: 不喝 bù hē, 不喜欢 bù xǐhuan.

blocks.title: Saying ‘no’
blocks.text: A short ‘no’ is the negated verb: 你有牛奶吗？— 没有。 你喝咖啡吗？— 不喝。 (S09)

askYourself: Is the verb 有 (have / there is)? → 没有 — never 不有.
Is the verb 是 (is)? → 不是 — never 没是.
Am I saying that something did not happen, or has not happened yet? → 没 + verb, without 了.
Is it a habit, a preference, a wish, a decision or the future? → 不 + verb.
Do I mean ‘no + noun’ (German kein)? → 没有 + the noun, without 一个.
Nothing, nobody, never? → 什么都 + 不 / 没 + verb; 没有人 at the start; 从来 + 不 / 没.
A second ‘not’ (nor)? → …，也不 + verb (也没 for facts and with 有).
Is the syllable after 不 in the 4th tone? → say bú.
steps: Find the verb (or the 在 + place phrase).
Choose 不 or 没 with the questions above.
Put the negator directly in front of it, after 都 / 也 / 从来 / 什么都; nothing else changes.
With 没有, drop 一 + measure word: 我有一瓶牛奶 → 我没有牛奶.

traps: *我不有牛奶 → 我没有牛奶.
*他没是老师 → 他不是老师.
*我没吃了 → 我没吃 (没 and 了 do not go together here).
不要 + verb is the command ‘don’t!’; ‘I don’t want to eat’ is 我不想吃.
Under 没有, 一个 normally disappears: 我没有苹果, not *我没有一个苹果.
*我不什么都吃 → 我什么都不吃.
*人没有在家 for ‘nobody is at home’ → 没有人在家.
*我从来吃肉 for ‘I never eat meat’ → 我从来不吃肉.

seeAlso.note: Arabic chooses the negator by tense and sentence type (lā, lam, lan, laysa, mā); Chinese chooses by meaning: 不 for will, habit and states, 没 for what did not happen and for 有.
Hebrew לֹא negates verbs and adjectives, אֵין says ‘there is not’ — much like the split between 不 and 没有.
German nicht vs kein depends on the noun (kein Brot = 没有面包); Chinese 不 vs 没 depends on time and aspect, and German nichts / niemand / nie need no nicht, while 什么都 / 没有人 / 从来 always come with 不 or 没.

quiz.why: 有 is negated only with 没, and 一 + measure word drops out.

quiz.q: ‘He doesn’t eat meat.’ (he is a vegetarian)
quiz.why: A habit or a choice → 不 before the verb.
Something that did not happen → 没, without 了.
什么都 before the negator; 没 for what did not happen (什么都不买 = she won’t buy anything).

quiz.q: How is 不 said in 不是?
